exam: What bedside questions differentiate a benign cyst from a malignant lump? — Look for sudden size change, pain, skin changes, systemic symptoms; benign cysts are usually painless and mobile.
A 28‑year‑old woman presents with a 2 cm mobile mass; ultrasound unavailable. What is your next step? — Perform FNAC to obtain cytology; if inconclusive, arrange referral for core biopsy.
How does tuberculous mastitis present differently from a typical breast abscess? — Often chronic, may have sinus formation, associated with HIV or TB elsewhere, and lacks acute systemic toxicity.

Why is cloxacillin preferred for lactational breast abscess in this setting? — It targets Staph aureus, is inexpensive, and has low resistance locally; avoid broad‑spectrum agents unless MRSA is common.
Explain the TNM T2 classification and its impact on surgical planning. — Tumour >2 cm ≤5 cm; may still be amenable to wide local excision but requires clear margins and possible sentinel node biopsy.
What red‑flag sign would make you refer a patient directly to oncology without waiting for biopsy results? — Fixed mass with skin ulceration or axillary node involvement suggesting advanced disease.

In a patient with known HIV, what additional investigation should you consider for a breast lump? — Test for TB (GeneXpert or acid‑fast stain) because TB mastitis is more common in immunocompromised patients.

How would you counsel a patient after excision of a benign fibro‑adenoma regarding future breast cancer risk? — Reassure that risk is not increased; advise regular self‑exam and routine clinical checks.
ai.title: Breast Lump Evaluation
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Breast lumps are common in low‑resource settings and range from benign fibro‑adenoma to cancer. Clinicians must use history, exam and limited investigations to triage and manage appropriately.

b: Palpable, discrete, mobile vs fixed
Associated skin or nipple changes
sections.p: A breast lump is any palpable or radiologically visible mass within breast tissue. Diagnosis begins with focused history and physical examination, followed by selective imaging or pathology.

b: T1 ≤2 cm, T2 >2 cm ≤5 cm, T3 >5 cm, T4 extension to chest wall/skin
N0 no nodes, N1 ipsilateral axillary nodes, N2 multiple nodes, N3 supraclavicular nodes
M0 no distant spread, M1 distant metastasis
sections.p: If cancer is suspected, stage using the TNM system (tumour size, nodal involvement, metastasis). Benign lesions have no stage.

b: Benign fibro‑adenoma (young women)
Fibrocystic change / cysts (reproductive age)
Breast abscess (often lactational, Staph aureus)
Tuberculous mastitis (HIV co‑infection)
Breast carcinoma (peak 40‑60 y, increasing incidence)
Phyllodes tumour (rare, can be malignant)

Fluctuant, tender → cyst or abscess
Redness, warmth, fever → infection

sections.p: Patients report a new lump, sometimes pain, discharge or skin changes. Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss) suggest infection or malignancy.

Cellular atypia present? → differentiates benign from malignant when histology unavailable
Histologic diagnosis of cancer? → determines treatment plan
Evidence of lung metastasis? → upstages disease
Immunosuppression present? → higher risk of TB mastitis, influences infection management

Axillary lymphadenopathy

b: Benign cyst – ultrasound‑guided aspiration, repeat if recurs
Fibro‑adenoma – observation; excision if >3 cm or symptomatic
Breast abscess – incision & drainage, empirical cloxacillin (covers Staph), adjust for MRSA if prevalent
Tuberculous mastitis – 6‑month anti‑TB regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol), surgical excision if sinus persists
Carcinoma – multidisciplinary plan: surgery (wide local excision or mastectomy), possible radiotherapy, chemotherapy (anthracycline‑based) if advanced; avoid hormone therapy in pregnancy
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; supportive care follows.

b: Benign lesions – review in 6 months, then annually
Abscess – wound check 48‑72 h, complete antibiotics course
TB mastitis – monitor liver function, ensure adherence
Cancer – post‑op review at 2 weeks, then every 3‑6 months; counsel on nutrition, limit alcohol, encourage early detection
sections.p: Schedule based on diagnosis; educate on self‑exam and risk reduction.

b: Lipoma – soft, mobile, subcutaneous
Chest wall sarcoma – deep, may involve ribs
Axillary lymphadenitis – node enlargement, not true breast tissue
Mastitis in lactating women – painful, erythematous, often bilateral
Ultrasound cystic appearance may hide solid tumour with necrotic centre

Chest X‑ray may miss small pulmonary mets; CT needed if suspicion high

Fever with rapidly enlarging painful lump
